---
title: "Electric Vehicles Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the Electric Vehicles activity, which combines per capita rates, correlation, regression, and small-multiples charts.

## Creating multiple new columns at once

```
vehicle_data <- vehicle_data |>
  mutate(
    Total_Registrations = Electric + Hybrid,
    Electric_per_1000 = (Electric / Population) * 1000,
    Hybrid_per_1000 = (Hybrid / Population) * 1000
  )
```

You can create several columns in a single `mutate()` call. Each line creates one column. R evaluates them in order, so later columns can reference earlier ones defined in the same call (though this example does not do that). Here, the per-1000 columns normalize the raw counts by population.

## Sorting with `arrange()`

```
vehicle_data |> arrange(desc(Electric_per_1000))
```

`arrange()` sorts rows. `desc()` means descending (highest first). Without `desc()`, it sorts ascending (lowest first). This is useful for finding which county has the highest per capita rate.

## Paired t-test

```
t_test <- t.test(vehicle_data$Electric, vehicle_data$Hybrid, paired = TRUE)
```

A *paired* t-test compares two measurements from the same units (here, electric and hybrid counts from the same counties). `paired = TRUE` tells R that the first value in `Electric` corresponds to the first value in `Hybrid`, and so on. This is different from an unpaired t-test, which treats the two groups as independent.

## Linear regression with `lm()`

```
model <- lm(Hybrid ~ Electric, data = vehicle_data)
summary(model)
```

`lm()` fits a linear regression. `Hybrid ~ Electric` means "predict Hybrid using Electric." The output from `summary(model)` includes coefficients (intercept and slope), R-squared (how much variation is explained), and p-values for each term.

## Working with residuals

```
residuals <- residuals(model)
summary(residuals)
```

`residuals(model)` extracts the difference between each actual value and what the model predicted. Large positive residuals mean the actual value was much higher than predicted; large negative residuals mean it was lower. `summary()` on residuals gives you the min, max, median, and quartiles.

## Adding predictions and residuals to the data

```
predictions <- predict(model, newdata = vehicle_data)
vehicle_data$Predicted_Hybrid <- predictions
vehicle_data$Residuals <- residuals
```

`predict()` generates the model's predicted values for each row. You can then add these as new columns using `$` assignment. This lets you see, row by row, what the model expected vs. what actually happened.

## Converting text dates with `ym()`

```
county_evs <- county_evs |>
  mutate(Year_Month = ym(Year_Month))
```

`ym()` is a `lubridate` function that converts a text string in year-month format (like "2023-06") into a proper date. Once converted, R can plot it correctly on a time axis and do date math. Other variants: `ymd()` for year-month-day, `mdy()` for month-day-year.

## Regression over time

```
model_electric <- lm(ELECTRIC ~ Year_Month, data = county_evs)
```

You can use a date column as a predictor in regression. R treats dates as numbers behind the scenes, so this asks: "as time moves forward, do electric vehicle registrations increase?" The slope tells you the average change per unit of time.

## Scatterplot with trend line using `geom_smooth()`

```
ggplot(county_evs, aes(x = Year_Month, y = ELECTRIC)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue")
```

`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` adds a linear trend line on top of the scatterplot. By default it also shows a gray confidence band. The trend line comes from the same type of linear regression you ran with `lm()`, just drawn directly on the chart.

## Small multiples with `facet_wrap()`

```
ggplot(vehicle_data, aes(x = Year_Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ELECTRIC, colour = "Electric")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = `PLUG-IN HYBRID`, colour = "Plug-In Hybrid")) +
  facet_wrap(~County)
```

`facet_wrap(~County)` creates a separate mini-chart for each county, all sharing the same axes. This makes it easy to compare trends across many groups at once. The `~` is required syntax — it tells `facet_wrap` which column to split on.

Two `geom_line()` layers are used to plot two different columns on the same chart. Each gets a different color label through the `colour` aesthetic, and `scale_color_manual()` controls the actual colors.

## Common mistakes

**Confusing `paired = TRUE` with an unpaired test:**

```
# Paired — compares the SAME counties' electric vs. hybrid counts:
t.test(vehicle_data$Electric, vehicle_data$Hybrid, paired = TRUE)

# Unpaired — treats them as unrelated groups (wrong here):
t.test(vehicle_data$Electric, vehicle_data$Hybrid)
```

Use `paired = TRUE` when both measurements come from the same units (same counties, same people, same schools). Use unpaired when the groups are independent.

**Forgetting `~` in `facet_wrap()`:**

```
# Error:
facet_wrap(County)

# Correct:
facet_wrap(~County)
```

The `~` is required — it is formula syntax that tells `facet_wrap()` which column to use for splitting.

**Adding predictions to the wrong data frame:**

```
# Wrong — adds columns to the original data, not the filtered version:
vehicle_data$Predicted <- predict(model_filtered)

# Correct — match predictions to the data the model was built on:
filtered_data$Predicted <- predict(model_filtered)
```

`predict(model)` generates one value per row in the data the model was trained on. If you try to attach those predictions to a different data frame with a different number of rows, you will get an error or mismatched data.
